title: Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment Comes to the Big Easy on September 14th
subtitle: An interview between Owen Muir, MD and Grady Hannah.
body_html:
Our live-action newsletter event, rapid acting mental health treatment, returns September 14th in New Orleans. I called my event cofounder Grady Hannah up to talk about it today, so you can get a sense of what's coming. This is just some of the flavor, even more is coming. People said a live action newsletter event would be stupid. When I say people, I mean me. But it turns out it was really good, and now we're coming up on our seventh event.

The news keeps being hot leading up to this event…

  • Former speaker Dr. Joshua Brown is the first Head of Brain Medicine.

  • Radial is Scaling.

  • Salma Health is offering specialized treatments for depression, anxiety, and even headache and facial pain. They are also hiring a ton!

  • BrainsWay accelerates its transdiagnostic potential with studies in stroke and a great feature video featuring Speaker Colleen Hanlon, Ph.D.—who will be doing an “ask the expert” opening to the event:

  • Psychiatric Times covers Brain Universal’s FDA cleared system for dry EEG in clinical practice.

  • EyeThree talks publicly about their qFMRI technology.

  • Definium’s Phase III Voyage Trial toplined!

  • Neurolief launches support for prescribers for patients using commercial insurance for ProlivRx— an at home treatment for depression after only one prior medication trial.

Enjoy the interview between myself and Grady below, where we talk about what's coming.

Stay tuned, get excited for more & see you in New Orleans! Also, we will have special guests. And surprises. And maybe….embarrassing merch, for me, personally.

Get your FREE RAMHT Tickets

Owen Muir: We have another Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment event coming up. Introduce yourself to our readers.

Grady Hannah: I’m Grady Hannah, co-founder of RAMHT, and I’ve been in psychiatry and digital therapeutics for over 10 years. Extremely excited for the upcoming event in New Orleans on September 14th.

Owen: We’re finally bringing RAMHT to the Big Easy.

Grady: Yes. A great local presence, plus people coming from all over. It’s our first show in New Orleans and we can’t wait.

Owen: Give the audience a little backstory on why It it was a great idea to bring this event to the big easy, and to open the invitation to professionals more broadly than just the psychiatrists who tend to attend APA?

Grady: The psychiatric nurse practitioner network is growing fast, and they’ve got a unique, pragmatic perspective. We have Andrew Penn as a speaker, one of the real stalwarts of that community. Many psych NPs come from other disciplines, so they bring practical experience relevant to psychiatry, or a different set of values that improve the care paradigm in ways that aren’t always obvious.

Owen: One example from my own experience. Guess how many blood draws I had to do in my medical school curriculum?

Grady: Zero.

Owen: Correct. I did dozens, then hundreds, through an elective emergency medicine procedure club. When I got to residency at Northwell, there was no weekend phlebotomist, and my classmates, with the standard zero venipunctures, were really lost. I wasn’t. A prior career in nursing or PA training gives you, I hate to call it more practical experience, but it’s more practical experience. What else makes nursing a great prelude to a subspecialty like psychiatry?

Grady: This is a group building their own practices. Psychiatrist MDs may be further down the rabbit hole of the cerebral and behavioral sides of the mind. Psych NPs look more at patient care and clinical operations, a little more patient-centric, and explore complementary areas of care to create new practices. I have my ideas about what this audience will be like, but that’s part of the excitement of a constituency that differs slightly from APA. I’m sure a lot will be familiar too.

Owen: This is also the first RAMHT meeting with robust, shareable data: finally, top-line phase three data on lysergide D-tartrate, otherwise known as LSD, from Definium’s Emerge study in major depressive disorder and Voyage study in generalized anxiety disorder. For the first time we’ll know what double-blind, randomized controlled trials look like. How does the data look to you?

Grady: The depression data is really powerful and has had a big impact. You see a lot of excited discussion. The anxiety data is very powerful too, but more overlooked. That’s what excites me, because it’s as if we’ve all decided that anxiety, even severe anxiety, is acceptable. And there aren’t great treatments for it.

Owen: Maybe that’s why we tolerate it. We have drugs we literally called antidepressants. Any clinician knows they often work, somewhat, for anxiety too, but even the name was antidepressants. Panic disorder got an FDA label; generalized anxiety disorder just didn’t have much of anything. And if you have nothing, it doesn’t make sense to focus where you can’t do any good.

Grady: Excellent point. I’m also very interested in the implications of LSD treatment. How are people going to be cared for during their treatment?

Owen: It’s a whole different business. They’re there for hours in a row.

Grady: And it’s coming soon.

Owen: Speaking of which: literally today, a secondary analysis from our colleagues at BrainsWay, from the SWIFT trial I was involved with, demonstrated rapid reductions in suicidality with accelerated deep TMS. The paradigm is similar: five hours a day for six half days, much like a psychedelic dosing day. Analysts are hand-wring about spending more than two hours in a clinic, but accelerated TMS patients have spent all day there for years, and it’s better for reducing suicidality. Relevant for this audience?

Grady: My wife, Mia, who’ll be speaking as a TMS advocate at the event, had a significant remission in her depression from an intensive one-day TMS treatment. Where LSD patients spend their treatment may look different than a typical clinic, but people are there for a therapeutic purpose. For many disease states, people have hospital stays much longer than a day. When you do the cost-benefit analysis, you fit the treatment to the cure. If that’s what’s necessary, we’ll adapt, as long as the data keeps looking this promising.

Owen: It’s like a good enterprise software pitch: they discuss your investment in the product, not your purchase. We’re investing time in remission from debilitating conditions. Framed as an investment in feeling well, it’s a little less hand-wringy.

Grady: They also talk about amortization. Intensive treatment over one day with a profound effect on your well-being likely beats taking an SSRI for years or decades.

Owen: And no one gripes about how long you spend on the golf course. Plenty of things get a full day and a blocked calendar.

Grady: Right. There’s a lot of movement in this space, and we want to keep current from the clinical, patient, and macro perspectives. You and Carlene are fantastic partners, and I can’t wait for the event.

Owen: I’m thrilled to say more soon, because we didn’t touch on novel diagnostic adjunctives: EEG and fMRI to understand what’s going on inside the brain before, during, and after these treatments.

Grady: It’s really two complementary categories, treatment planning and objective diagnostic analysis. TMS targeting, understanding the effects of TMS pulses on the brain: it’s important quantitative data, because as an industry we want objective inputs and outputs that show standard of care, so psychiatry gets payment schedules representative of interventional brain medicine using state-of-the-art tools. There are newer, vertically integrated companies in dry EEG (hardware, software, and diagnostic), plus traditional players finding their way. A lot of intersection happening.

Owen: I look forward to folks joining us September 14th in New Orleans to learn about these rapid, and more importantly, more effective, treatments and diagnostics for brain disorders.

Grady: Can’t wait, and be there early. The first attendees are entered in a raffle for a limited edition Owen Muir bobblehead. If you want a little more Owen in your life, it’s possible. Not life-size, unfortunately. Please join us.

Owen: The pint-size Muir bobblehead is real, and prompt arrival enters you in the raffle. This is so embarrassing.

Get your FREE RAMHT Tickets

Thanks for reading. Hope to see you there!

BK Historic House and GardensNew Orleans, LA

Monday, September 14 • 5 PM - 9 PM
